reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive near-total absence of metabolically active adipose tissue evident from birth or early infancy, producing a strikingly muscular, prominent-veined appearance
Commonest subtypes arise from AGPAT2 (triglyceride synthesis) and BSCL2/seipin (adipocyte differentiation) mutations, with CAV1 and PTRF/CAVIN1 causing rarer variants
Very low circulating leptin drives voracious appetite, and fat that cannot be stored subcutaneously accumulates ectopically in liver and muscle
Severe insulin resistance with acanthosis nigricans, marked hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis with hepatomegaly, and early-onset diabetes are characteristic
Acromegaloid features, prominent musculature, umbilical prominence, and in some subtypes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or intellectual impairment (BSCL2) may occur
Leptin (metreleptin) replacement is a cornerstone therapy in leptin-deficient generalised lipodystrophy, improving glycaemia, triglycerides, and hepatic fat
Recurrent pancreatitis from extreme hypertriglyceridaemia is a major avoidable complication
Diagnosis integrates the generalised fat-loss pattern, very low leptin, the metabolic panel, and confirmatory genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital generalised lipodystrophy is an inherited near-total failure to develop or maintain functional adipose tissue, caused by biallelic mutations in genes governing triglyceride synthesis (AGPAT2), lipid-droplet/adipocyte formation (BSCL2/seipin), or caveolar structure (CAV1, PTRF/CAVIN1). Without a normal fat depot, dietary and endogenous lipid cannot be stored subcutaneously and is deposited ectopically in liver, skeletal muscle, and other organs, driving profound insulin resistance. The tiny fat mass secretes very little leptin, removing satiety signalling and provoking hyperphagia that worsens the lipid overload. The resulting phenotype combines hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and early insulin-resistant diabetes.
additionalDifferentials: Familial partial lipodystrophy presenting in childhood
Leprechaunism/Donohue syndrome and other extreme INSR defects
Mandibuloacral dysplasia with generalised fat loss
Poorly controlled type 1 diabetes with marked wasting
additionalInvestigations: Serum leptin (characteristically very low) and fasting insulin/C-peptide to document insulin resistance
Fasting lipid profile focusing on triglycerides, and glucose/HbA1c for diabetes
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging to assess steatosis and hepatomegaly
Whole-body or regional fat imaging (MRI/DEXA) to map the near-total fat deficit
Targeted genetic testing of AGPAT2, BSCL2, CAV1, and PTRF/CAVIN1
Echocardiography where a cardiomyopathy-associated subtype is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive fatty liver toward steatohepatitis and cirrhosis
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia in susceptible subtypes
Uncontrolled insulin-resistant diabetes with severe hyperglycaemia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on metabolic control; leptin (metreleptin) replacement and aggressive management of triglycerides and glucose substantially improve outcomes, but untreated disease carries risks of pancreatitis, progressive liver disease, and cardiac complications.
pitfalls: Attributing the muscular, veiny habitus to athleticism and missing the diagnosis
Overlooking very low leptin as the key discriminating biochemical clue
Underestimating pancreatitis risk when triglycerides are extremely high
Assuming standard insulin regimens will control the diabetes despite severe resistance
Failing to arrange genetic confirmation and family counselling
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on lipodystrophy
management: Metreleptin (recombinant leptin) replacement is the disease-specific cornerstone in leptin-deficient generalised lipodystrophy, improving glycaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis and hyperphagia
Treat the severe insulin-resistant diabetes with high-dose insulin regimens and insulin sensitisers such as metformin
Aggressively lower triglycerides with fibrates and omega-3 fatty acids to reduce the risk of pancreatitis
Institute a controlled, low-fat balanced diet with dietitian input to limit ectopic lipid accumulation
Monitor and manage hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis, and screen for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and other organ complications with echocardiography where indicated
Manage acute severe hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis promptly and consider apheresis for extreme hypertriglyceridaemia
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for autosomal recessive AGPAT2, BSCL2, CAV1 and CAVIN1 inheritance, and coordinate specialist endocrine and metabolic care
